en: The Diagram for Distinguishing Excesses and Confusions Regarding the Five Teachings, the Abandonment and Realization, and the Three Awakenings of the Venerable Master Xianshou,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuzha of Qingzhou and Cizhou, with the assistance of his disciple Yanzhi, based on the Tripiṭaka transmitted from the East;

it was only during the Tang dynasty that this became complete, as the patriarchs’ classifications of the teachings reached their full scope through the venerable Xianshou’s exhaustive exegesis of the scriptures.

Since these works are numerous, one’s knowledge and vision naturally broaden. By analyzing the meanings and judging the teachings, what was incomplete becomes fully prepared; thus, each subsequent work excels the preceding ones.

The twenty-odd treatises of Xianshou, the fifty-odd treatises of Qingliang, and the ten-odd treatises of Guishan all provide detailed expositions on the teachings, contemplation, severance, and realization.

This is especially true for the severance and realization within the Five Teachings, which originally derive from the sūtras and śāstras; while the former have not yet appeared, the latter are complete.
The stream has reached us, yet people have not examined it; instead, they say there is neither judgment nor realization. Is this not to suppress and belittle the Buddhas and Patriarchs?

(Continued Dharma) Feeling this in my heart as a source of pain, I have accordingly excerpted the judgments and realizations from the various great treatises of the Xianzong school, arranging them in charts and connecting them with lines.
I hope that students, through the definitive explanations of this single school, will understand them as clearly as looking at their own palms, free from even the slightest doubt or obstruction.

If they can truly give rise to the initial aspiration and proceed to the perfect, wondrous enlightenment—ensuring that every aspect of their understanding and practice within this path is unerring—they will ultimately sever the barriers of attachment in the Lotus Treasury World and realize the Dharma-realm within the nature-ocean of Vairocana. Whether progressing gradually or leaping suddenly, what difficulty could there be?

Ah! This is merely a brief indication of its general outline. If one wishes for a detailed understanding, one should consult the various treatises on the ritual of the teachings regarding the three types of awakening.
While the three stages differ in their positions, the single nature of awakening is identical; it is simply by being able to awaken to this that one suddenly perfects the wondrous awakening.

The stage of original enlightenment (*benjue*) is non-enlightened according to all five teachings. The stage of perfect enlightenment (*yuanjue*) corresponds, at the minimum, to the stages of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*;

the latter four [teachings] regard it as the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miaojue*). The stage of initial enlightenment (*shijue*) extends from the first arousal of the mind up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*dengjue*). Within this, there are further three positions:

First, the position of enlightenment by name (*mingzi juewei*), which spans from the initial arousal of the mind to the stage of "stopping the mind" (*tingxin*); both initial and equal enlightenment correspond here to the ten levels of faith (*shixin*). Second...

The stage of similar awakening (*sadr̥śa-bodhi*) extends from the minor distinct characteristics (*pr̥thak-lakṣaṇa*) up to the supreme mundane dharma (*laukika-agra-dharma*); subsequently, the four [stages] correspond to the three levels of the noble ones (*ārya*) and the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*).

The stage of partial awakening (*yathābhāga-bodhi*) extends from the minor first fruit (*phala*) up to the third fruit; it begins with the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth, corresponding to perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

The differences in their relative heights and gradations are unequal, and they are explained according to the specific teachings regarding what is abandoned and realized. Therefore, these three awakenings... the five... [are established].
Position: This is capable of discerning the provisional and the real within the characteristics of the teachings.
The One Vehicle’s uncommon teaching is the inexhaustible, wondrously enlightened fundamental Buddha-nature, the unobstructed Dharma-realm.
(This is the Perfect Teaching [yuanjiao]. Regarding its severance and realization, it is like unraveling a brocade flower, or like melting a golden lion.)

(From the First Abode to the Sublime. The number of chapters follows that of the final [section]. However, these three stages—Transcendence, Suddenness, and Sublimity—directly reach Perfect Enlightenment, thus comprising sixty-two chapters.
[Essential Nature] Non-awakening (meaning non-awakening to the nature of the Dharma-realm) [Name]
Generating the Mind (referring to generating the mind of the vast and great practices and vows of Samantabhadra):

Initial Faith (eliminates the manifest aspects of both conceptual and innate ego-clinging; it is equal to the first fruit of the Small Vehicle, the beginning of the First Ground, the end of the First Dwelling, and the seven faiths of the sudden path).

Seventh Faith (eliminates the manifest aspects of both conceptual and innate clinging to dharmas; it is equal to the fourth fruit of the Small Vehicle, the beginning of the Seventh Ground, the end of the Seventh Dwelling, and the beginning of the First Dwelling of the sudden path).

The Nine Faiths (subdue the coarse seeds of both the discriminative and innate grasping at the two attachments; they correspond to the initial stage of Subtle Enlightenment [the First Ground] and the final two stages of Practice [the Eighth through Tenth Grounds], being simultaneous with the Seventh Abode).

The Ten Faiths (subdue the subtle seeds of both the discriminative and innate grasping at the two attachments; they correspond to the final ten stages of Practice and are simultaneous with the ten Abodes). [These are the "Similar" stages. (The above clarify the "round" subduing of the intermediate and the subduing of the coarse; the following clarify the "perfect" severance.)

The First Abiding (removes the coarse seeds of both the conceptual and innate grasping at the two [self-natures]; it is equal to the final stage of the Ten Directions and the initial stage of the Ten Practices).
The Ten Abidings (removes the subtle seeds of both the conceptual and innate grasping at the two; it is equal to the final stage of the Ten Directions and the initial stage of the Ten Practices).

The Initial Practice (perfectly severs the manifest and seed-states of both the conceptual and innate grasping at the two, exhausting them entirely; further severing a portion of the habitual tendencies, it is equal to the final stage of the First Ground and the initial stage of the First Direction).

The Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*): [One] perfectly severs eleven portions of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the two attachments; [this stage] is equal to the final Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), which is identical to the first *bhūmi*.

The Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*): [One] perfectly severs twenty portions of the habitual tendencies; [this stage] is equal to the sudden realization of the ten *bhūmis*. The Four Additions (*catasraḥ prayogāḥ*):
[One] perfectly severs the remaining habitual tendencies of the ten practices; [one] then proceeds to sever the habitual tendencies of the first *bhūmi*.
[According to the degrees:
The First Bhūmi (completely eliminates twenty-one parts of habitual tendencies; equal to the Sudden Perfect Enlightenment);
The Second Bhūmi (completely eliminates twenty-two parts of habitual tendencies; equal to the Sudden Sublime Enlightenment).
The Third Ground (*bhūmi*) [perfectly severs twenty-three portions of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*]. In the Sudden Teaching, the specific names are not known).
Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) [perfectly severs thirty-one portions of the habitual tendencies; further severing one portion of the habitual tendencies of the Buddha-ground].

Perfect Enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) [perfectly severs the two attachments, exhausting the infinite manifest seeds and habitual tendencies. Abiding in the soil of the unobstructed *dharmadhātu*, becoming a Buddha of the unobstructed *dharmadhātu*, seated upon the universally harmonious and inexhaustible lion throne, he expounds the conditions].

[This refers to] the arising of the Dharma-realm teachings that transform the biased instructions for the three vehicles, as well as those of ordinary beings and non-Buddhists of the highest faculties, so that their biases are rectified into the [perfect] diagram.
○ Sudden Teaching (The severance and realization of this teaching are like the ceasing of madness and delusion, or like awakening from a dream).
[In this section, the chapters follow the preceding model; here, the three stages likewise transcend the ultimate subtlety, increasing to form fifty-two chapters.]
[Text] Non-awakening (meaning non-awakening to the nature of *tathatā*) [Title] Arousing the Mind (meaning arousing the mind of internally realized noble wisdom).

The first stage of faith (subdues the manifest forms of both the conceptual and innate grasping at the two [self-entities]; it corresponds to the preparatory stage of the Śrāvakas, beginning with the first and ending equal to the tenth stage of faith).

The seventh stage of faith (eliminates the manifest forms of the conceptual and innate grasping at a self; it corresponds to the first fruit of the Śrāvaka, beginning from the first bhūmi and ending equal to the first abiding).
(The above all involve sudden subdual; those below all involve sudden abandonment; this section clarifies both subdual and abandonment.)

[Similarity: The first dwelling (excluding the manifest conceptual and innate grasping at dharmas; equal to the four small fruits of the śrāvaka and the first seven stages up to the seventh dwelling);

the seventh dwelling (subduing the coarse seeds of both conceptual and innate grasping at the two [self and phenomena]; equal to the initial state of wondrous enlightenment and the final two practices).

The Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*): [one] subdues the subtle seeds of both the discriminative and innate grasping at the two [extremes]; [this stage] is equal to the final [stage of] the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*). The First Practice (*prathama-caryā*):

[one] eliminates the coarse seeds of both the discriminative and innate grasping at the two [extremes]; [this stage] is equal to the initial [stage of] the Ten Approaches (*daśa-prayoga*). The Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*):
[one] eliminates the subtle seeds of both the discriminative and innate grasping at the two [extremes]; [this stage] is equal to the final [stage of] the Ten Approaches.

The Ten Faiths (*śraddhācaryā*): [One] suddenly severs both the dualistic grasping of conceptualization and its innate counterparts, as well as their manifest and seed forms; furthermore, one severs a portion of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), reaching parity with the end of the first stage (*bhūmi*). The Ten Abodes (*vihāra*):
[One] suddenly severs ten portions of the habitual tendencies of the dualistic grasping, reaching parity with the end of the tenth stage.
The Four Additional Practices (*prayoga*): One severs the remaining habitual tendencies of the preceding ten abodes and advances to suppress the habitual tendencies of the first stage.
[According to the respective stages:
The First Ground (suddenly severs eleven portions of habitual tendencies; equal to the ultimate Perfect Enlightenment);

the Second Ground (suddenly severs twelve portions of habitual tendencies; equal to the ultimate Sublime Enlightenment); from the Third Ground onward, the names [of these stages] are not known in the Final Teaching.

Samyaksaṃbodhi (Equal Enlightenment): [Sudden] one simultaneously severs twenty-one parts of the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the stages; subsequently, one severs the remaining one part of the habit-energies of the Buddha-stage.

[Perfect] Prabhāsvarabodhi (Wondrous Enlightenment): One simultaneously severs the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*), exhausting all present seeds and habit-energies. Abiding in the Dharma-nature Land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*), one becomes a Dharma-nature Buddha (*dharmatā-buddha*). Seated upon the throne of empty space, one preaches the Dharma of the True Nature of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna-tattva-dharma*), causing those of the gradual teachings of the three vehicles, as well as ordinary beings of superior faculties and followers of external paths, to transform their gradual practice into the sudden.
○ The Final Teaching (In this teaching, the severance and realization are like gold being formed from ore, or water remaining as water [in its true nature];
that is, from the First Abode up to the Ultimate [Abode], there are forty-two stages in each, which should be understood as superior to the Initial Teaching).
[Text] Non-awakening (meaning non-awakening to the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha);
[Title] Arising of the Mind (meaning the arising of a profound, upright mind of compassion).
The first stage of faith (which briefly subdues the two obstacles);

the seventh stage of faith (subduing the coarse manifest aspects of both the discriminative and innate forms of the two obstacles, which is equal to the general characteristics of the Śrāvaka path and begins at the same level as the ten stages of dedication);

the tenth stage of faith (subduing the subtle manifest aspects of both the discriminative and innate forms of the two obstacles, which is equal to the Śrāvaka path of application and begins at the same level as the first stage).
[Similarity: The first dwelling (removing afflictive conceptual and innate manifestations; equal to the small first fruit and the initial stage);
the seventh dwelling (removing cognitive conceptual and innate manifestations; equal to the small fourth fruit and the initial seventh stage).

Second Stage (Subdues the coarse seeds of both the discriminative and innate afflictions of the two obstacles; equal to the initial wondrous enlightenment. From the third stage onward, those of the Initial Teaching do not know this designation.
Tenth Stage (Subdues the subtle seeds of both the discriminative and innate afflictions of the two obstacles.
First Orientation (Eliminates the coarse seeds of both the discriminative and innate afflictions of the two obstacles.)
The ten dedications (removing the subtle seeds of both the conceptual and innate obstacles);
the four stages of application (subduing the habitual tendencies of both obstacles).
[The above clarify the state of possessing both the subduing and the severing of the two obstacles; from here on, it concerns the state of possessing both the severing and the subduing.]
[To a certain extent:

On the first bhūmi (the exhaustion of both the dual obstacles—conceptual and innate—along with their manifest and latent seeds, followed by the further abandonment of one portion of their habitual tendencies);
on the ten bhūmis (the abandonment of ten portions of the habitual tendencies of the two obstacles).

Samyaksaṃbodhi (Equal Enlightenment): [The stage of] severing eleven parts of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obstacles; [further] advancing to sever one part of the habitual tendencies of the Buddha-ground.

[Perfect] Samyaksambuddha (Perfect Enlightenment): The exhaustion of the manifest, seeds, and habitual tendencies of the two obstacles. Abiding in the Saṃbhogakāya realm, he becomes a Saṃbhogabuddha. Seated upon the Vajrāsana, he proclaims the Dharma of the Tathāgatagarbha, causing those of the provisional teachings of the three vehicles, as well as ordinary persons and non-Buddhists of medium capacity, to transform the provisional into the real.
○ Initial Teaching (In this teaching, the severance and realization are like a mirror free from defilement, or like the moon emerging from clouds).

[It severs the two obstacles of phenomena and principle; it extinguishes the two deaths of partial transformation and full transformation; it reveals the principles of the two emptinesses of self and dharmas; it realizes the two fruits of wisdom and severance. From the first stage up to the ultimate, there are twelve grades in each.]
[Text] Non-awakening (meaning non-awakening to the dharma-nature of the two kinds of emptiness);
[Name] Arising of the Resolve (meaning the arousal of the mind to practice and deliver sentient beings).
The Ten Faiths (initially subduing the two obstacles;
[analogous]) The Ten Abidings (doubly subduing the two obstacles; therein, slightly subduing the afflictions of conceptualized manifestations)
The Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*) [within the stage of "Simultaneous Subduing of the Two Obstructions"]: slightly subdue the manifest conceptualizations of the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

The Ten Dedications (*daśa-pratipatti*): subdue and eliminate the manifest conceptualizations of both obstructions; they correspond to the "Provisions" (*sambhāra*), "Emptiness," and "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*), and are equal to the "General Recollection of Small Scope.

The Four Additions (*catasraḥ prakarṣa-gatayaḥ*): eliminate the manifest conceptualizations of both obstructions, and subdue the seeds of conceptualization as well as the manifest [afflictions] of innate [ignorance]; they correspond to the "Addition to Practice" (*prakarṣa-caryā*), the "Stage of Emptiness" (*śūnyatā-bhūmi*), and are equal to the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) of the Small Vehicle.
[To a certain extent:

The First Ground (initially severs the seeds of the two obstacles of conceptualization; subsequently severs a portion of the seeds and manifestations of the innate [obstacles]. The Path of Vision of Characteristics, the Stage of the Eight Persons, and the Stage of Seeing are equal to the first fruit of the Lesser Vehicle).
The Third Ground (severs three parts of the seeds and manifestations of the innate two obstacles. This is the Stage of Thinning Desire. It is equal to the second fruit of the Lesser Vehicle).

The Fifth Ground (the stage of abandoning the seeds and manifestations of the two obstacles that arise simultaneously; the ground of emptiness and freedom from desire; equal to the third fruit of the Small Vehicle).

The Seventh Ground (the stage of abandoning the seeds and manifestations of the two obstacles that arise simultaneously; the ground of emptiness and having already accomplished what was to be done; equal to the fourth fruit of the Small Vehicle).

The Eighth Ground (the stage of abandoning the seeds and manifestations of the two obstacles that arise simultaneously; the ground of emptiness and the stage of the Pratyekabuddha; equal to the Pratyekabuddha of the Small Vehicle).

The Ninth Ground (*navamī-bhūmi*): [one] eliminates nine portions of the seeds and manifestations of the two obstacles that arise simultaneously (*sahaja*). [This level] is equal to the fruit of a Lesser Buddha; the Lesser Vehicle teachings do not know its name. The Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samāyogi-bodhi*): [one] eliminates eleven portions of the seeds and manifestations of the two obstacles that arise simultaneously.

One further eliminates one portion of the Buddha-ground. [At this stage,] the aspect of the Bodhisattva ground is empty; it is the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*). [Perfect] Wondrous Enlightenment (*vimala-sambodhi*):

[one] suddenly eliminates all seeds and manifestations of both the discriminative and simultaneous aspects of the two obstacles. The aspect of the Buddha-ground is empty; it is the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*). Residing in the Pure Land of Transformation, one becomes a Supreme Response-Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*). Seated upon a throne of celestial robes, one expounds the Dharma of the emptiness of aspects.
This causes those of the Lesser Vehicle, ordinary persons of inferior faculties, and non-Buddhists to transform the small into the great.
○ The Small Teaching (In this teaching, the severance and realization are like wood turning to ash, or form returning to emptiness;
it severs the afflictive hindrances, extinguishes death in segmented succession, reveals the principle of the emptiness of sentient beings, and realizes the fruit of partial truth).

[Text] Non-awakening (the stage of ordinary beings; although the nature of awakening is inherently present, it becomes non-awakening due to the obscuring delusion of ignorance; this is non-awakening that is biased toward the true nature).
[Title] Arising of the Mind (meaning the production of the mind that seeks to leave the realm of transmigration and attain extinction).

The Five Stopping Minds (*pañca-vinodana-citta*): [for those with] excessive greed, the contemplation of impurity; for excessive anger, the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion; for excessive delusion, the contemplation of causes and conditions; for excessive distraction, the contemplation of counting the breaths; for excessive hindrances, the contemplation of the Buddha. This stage destroys the hindrances. [The Stage of] Similarity:

Contemplating the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-smṛti*): contemplating the body as impure, contemplating sensations as suffering, contemplating the mind as impermanent, and contemplating phenomena as selfless.

The stage of mindfulness of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*): [One contemplates that the body is impure; that sensation, mind, and phenomena are all impure; and so on, up to contemplating that phenomena are selfless, and that body, sensation, mind, and phenomena are likewise selfless.

(These two preceding stages involve contemplating only the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to suppress the afflictions and delusions. (The above constitutes the stage of equipment [*sambhārāvasthā*].)
*Uṣmagata* (Heat): [One] first contemplates the Four Truths of the Desire Realm, cultivating the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).
*Mūrdhan* (Summit): [One] uses contemplation as before;

it becomes increasingly clear and lucid. *Kṣānti* (Patience): *Mṛdu-kṣānti* (Lower Patience): One universally contemplates the eight truths, cultivating thirty-two aspects. *Madhya-kṣānti* (Middle Patience): One gradually reduces the objects and aspects until only one aspect remains for two moments.
(Upper Patience also contemplates only the suffering of the desire realm. Within one aspect and two moments, the first moment is exhausted.
The Supreme Worldly Dharma (within one aspect and two moments, the latter moment is exhausted; it suppresses and eliminates conceptual afflictions). (The above constitutes the stage of application.)
The *srotāpanna* (who has severed the eighty-eight afflictions of conceptual views pertaining to the three realms; the stage of penetration).
The *sakṛdāgāmin* (who has severed the first six categories of innate afflictions of the desire realm).

Anāgāmin (having severed the final three categories of afflictions in the desire realm and further severing the seventy-two categories of innate afflictions of the two upper realms; the above constitutes the stage of cultivation).

[Round] Arhat (one who has exhausted both the afflictions of conceptual and innate grasping at a self, realized the principle of the emptiness of persons, and dwells in either nirvana with or without remainder; the stage of No-more-learning).

[Round] Pratyekabuddhas [belong to the stage of] No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa). They sever the afflictive hindrances of both views and mental formations (dṛṣṭi-kleśa-āvaraṇa), which is the same as the Śrāvakas; however, they further penetrate the residual habitual tendencies (vāsanā), and thus they rank above them. The remaining principles and fruits are likewise the same.

[Round] The Buddha (from the first aspiration, he made the Four Great Vows; through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and one hundred *kalpas*, he cultivated various marks and characteristics; subsequently entering the stage of the *upapatti-bhūmi* [the stage of being next to Buddhahood], he took birth in a womb, left home, and sat unmoving; he gave rise to true *anāsrava* [outflow-free] wisdom, suddenly severing the afflictions of *darśana-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya* along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Abiding in a defiled land of transformation, he became an inferior response-body Buddha (*pratirūpaka-buddha*), sitting upon a seat of grass and preaching the Dharma of the Truths and Conditions, causing the lowest-of-the-low ordinary beings and non-Buddhists to transform from the mundane into the sacred [the stage of no-more-learning]).
In the spring of the Gengxu year, I inscribed this diagram on a single sheet of paper.

Since members of both the monastic and lay communities might easily lose it if it were not affixed to the side of their seats, I respectfully requested a calligrapher to transcribe it again in horizontal lines onto a book page on the eighth day of the twelfth month of the Xinyou year.
This ensures that it may be consulted whether sitting or walking, and furthermore, that it may circulate far and wide for a long time. However—
The observer must not remain stagnant in the Buddha. If one views this as being deluded regarding the root and chasing after the branches:

vertically, it proceeds from the upper first to the lower last; horizontally, it proceeds from the front first to the back last. If one views this as returning to the truth from delusion: vertically, it proceeds from the lower last to the upper first;
horizontally, it proceeds from the back last to the front first. People only know of the small, the beginning, the end, the gradual, and the sudden, but they do not know the Perfect [Teaching].

The *Tonshūshi-shō* (Abridged Account of the Beginning and End) was originally small; I have now specially illustrated it here, arranging it into two sections so that one may see its sequential unfolding while realizing that, in essence, it is perfectly integrated and unimpeded.
Written by the practitioner Jikaku Daishi Kanjō at Zuiun-ji.
